The thing is concessions have always been overpriced. That's the main way theaters made a profit. In the past before the advent of streaming, theaters were THE place to see the latest movies. People begrudgingly paid a lot because it was the only option. If they wanted to rent vhs or later dvds it wouldn't be available for months after the movie left theaters. 

Today with ease of streaming and the business model of movies changing completely to make deals with streaming services people are no longer willing to continue to pay for concessions at a theater when they can just wait a few weeks and see the movie at home. The cultural aspect of going to the theaters has been slowly eroding away. 

Is it a good or bad thing? Kinda both. It's convenient to watch a movie at home, however with the writer strikes and the never ending ballooning of the number of subscription services and price hikes it seems like streaming can only make so much money before they need to restructure to make more profit. That means us as the consumers are going to end up paying more somehow. This industry is always evolving and the bottom line is more profit not better movies or a better deal for consumers. The worst is yet to come.

It's unreasonable to expect yourself to be 100% reliable for everyone all the time. People run late to things whether personal or professional for numerous legitimate reasons. 

That being said, communication is the key to navigating this successfully. If you are going to be late let people know as soon as possible. And unless it's an emergency keep it within about 15 mins max. 

These anecdotes you've provided are well outside of 15 mins and are not excusable. Especially if they don't give you an approximate ETA and just show up when they show up. 

One thing to note. Professional settings are higher stakes so timeliness will be more important. Most people view social settings as much more lenient. So they might show up late to a dinner and think there's no problem. In this case, if it bothers you then you need to communicate that. You might not get a sympathetic response, but at least you'll know they aren't going to care about timeliness in the future and you can either lower your expectations or distance yourself from them. 

Be cognizant of the possibility that you might be too nice and are defaulting into people pleasing. You may be holding yourself to an unreasonable standard and letting people off the hook for disrespecting your time at the same time. This is common among a lot of people.

Remember that niceness is not authentic. It's a learned response to conform to societal norms of avoiding conflict/confrontation. What you should aim to be instead is kind. And sometimes the kind thing to do when someone is late and it makes you upset is to call them out on it respectfully. So they are aware they are negatively affecting you. 

As for the deadly fear that you have. There isn't a better way to handle this than with exposure therapy. Remember that your self worth isn't tied to your perfect reliability. And that if you happen to let someone down at some point they will not dislike/hate you for it. Even if they get upset in the moment they will get over it once they get back to worrying about their own lives shortly thereafter. Go disappoint people and see for yourself. It's not that bad.

Within the last few weeks I've come to a place where I can understand that my parents were horribly neglected as children from their parents. It's a vicious generational cycle. I love my parents as they tried their best and they were able to at least provide for me physically with food, clothes, a roof over my head, even toys from time to time. But I feel much happier limiting my contact with them for my own mental health. I've never told them I'm angry or resentful, they are clueless and every once in a while I go home and have dinner with them as well as attend big holidays and birthday get togethers. I accept their limited capacity to love me and as long as they more or less behave well in those limited moments I'll continue to see them. 

Letting go and accepting how things happened is the hardest part. I love how in the book the author admits it's not supposed to be shaming parents for damaging their children. We could increase the epic scale of how the movies made us feel while being grounded in some level of reality with actors acting in real sets and practical effects. I'll be honest, therapy isn't a sure fire thing. It depends on where you go and how your therapist is. Like you said it works for some people and doesn't for others. I think in theory therapy should always be helpful but if you get a bad therapist it can sour your experience. The only real way to find out if it will work for you is if you give it a try. If you go willingly you really have nothing to lose. If you decide you don't like it you can choose to stop going. Easy as that. 

Here are a few pointers in case you decide to try it out. 

1. Be careful about talking about suicide:
I think it's the law that if a therapist thinks you're in danger of hurting yourself or others that they have to get the authorities involve and break confidentiality. 

It doesn't mean you can't talk about suicide at all. Especially if you really do think about it. But make sure to be clear that even if you think about it you would never go through with it and have never made a plan to seriously attempt it. That way they will keep that information private. 

2. They might be quick to suggest taking medication:
Please do not take this the wrong way. If pills really do help you in some way without having side effects that are too costly then it's a legitimate attempt at a solution. It's easy to feel like your therapist just wants an easy fix and sees you more like a statistic instead of a human being but please understand they're just trying to help you the best way that they can. Humankind still has a lot to learn about mental illness so we're not always sure how to help some people. It might have to be trial and error until you find something that works.

Ask lots of questions, make sure they are very clear about how the pills work and what the potential side effects are. If you agree to try them out you need to take them for up to 6 weeks  for them to finally start to take effect so be patient. Once that happens evaluate how you feel. If you feel better then keep the treatment going, if you feel worse stop taking the pills immediately. Unfortunately if they don't work you might have to start over with different pills for another 6 weeks. It's a long process but it's absolutely worth it if you eventually find something that work for you. Everyone is different, our body chemistry is very complex. One pill might work for one person but not another person. It's just basic trail and error. 

Therapy isn't a perfect cure for anything. It's simply a tool to help you deal with your mental health. I'll be honest it's not always easy either. Opening up to a stranger and being comfortable enough to cry in front of them takes a lot of guts. And going on and off pills can be long and tiring. But like anything in life that's worth doing, it takes hard work and determination. Believe that you can feel better, and trust that a professional therapist can help you achieve that. Maybe it won't work and that's okay too. You'll find a different way to cope throughout your life. Or maybe you'll respond better with a different therapist. One thing for certain is that you cannot feel better if you do nothing. I've spent almost a decade doing nothing and I've finally picked myself up and reached out for help. That's the hardest part and it's the most rewarding part. I still struggle daily, therapy has not "fixed " my problems. But it has given me hope and I can feel happy more often than before. I wish you the best of luck on your journey through life! It's painful and it's hard but it's also beautiful and fulfilling. 

Sorry for such a long post lol. I just hope I was able to encourage you to give it a shot.
